action: Replace self-signed, expired, weak or untrusted certificates with certificates issued by a trusted authority, with a name matching the service and an RSA key of at least 2048 bits.
Disable SSL 2.0/3.0, TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1; allow only TLS 1.2 and 1.3.
Remove weak cipher suites (RC4, 3DES, NULL, EXPORT, anonymous) and prefer ECDHE suites with AES-GCM or ChaCha20.
Use Diffie-Hellman groups of at least 2048 bits, or ECDHE.
Plan to enable hybrid post-quantum key exchange (ML-KEM) as soon as the products concerned support it.
Add the HTTP Strict-Transport-Security header on HTTPS services.
Add the Content-Security-Policy (frame-ancestors) or X-Frame-Options headers.
Set the Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite attributes on session cookies.
Disable the HTTP TRACE and TRACK methods.
Disable directory listing.
Remove diagnostic pages and backup files that are accessible from the web.

Remove weak algorithms from sshd_config (CBC ciphers, SHA-1/MD5 MACs, diffie-hellman-group1/14-sha1 key exchanges) and apply the fix for Terrapin (disable ChaCha20-Poly1305 and EtM modes if no update is available).
Disable the Telnet service (passwords are sent in clear text) and administer devices over SSH.

titre: Replace weak or default SSH keys
action: Regenerate the SSH host keys and remove static or published keys from authorized_keys files.

titre: Disable the r* services (rlogin, rsh, rexec)
action: Disable rlogin, rsh and rexec and use SSH.
Replace default or easily guessed SNMP community strings, restrict SNMP access to monitoring stations and switch to SNMPv3.
Limit recursion to authorised internal clients and prohibit unauthorised zone transfers.
Disable NTP control queries (mode 6/7) from outside (restrict default noquery).
Isolate IPMI interfaces on a dedicated administration network, disable cipher 0 and change the default accounts.
Protect VNC with a strong password and an encrypted tunnel, or disable the service.
Prohibit unauthenticated X11 connections (xhost -) or disable network listening on the X server.
Limit NFS exports to authorised hosts and remove world-readable shares.
Enable authentication and restrict network access to the databases concerned to the application servers only.
Immediately change the default or blank passwords of the accounts detected.
Refuse open relay and enforce STARTTLS.
Filter ICMP timestamp messages (types 13 and 14) on the local or network firewall.
Block mDNS (UDP 5353) outside the local segment or disable the service if it is not needed.
Disable UPnP or block SSDP (UDP 1900) outside the local segment.
Disable IP forwarding (net.ipv4.ip_forward = 0) if the machine does not act as a router.
Check that this DHCP server is legitimate and authorised on this segment; otherwise, disable it.
Block SNMP (UDP 161) from outside and restrict it to monitoring stations, or disable it if unused, to prevent its use in reflection attacks (GETBULK requests).

Identify the applications and protocols that send credentials in cleartext over the network (HTTP, FTP, Telnet, POP, IMAP, LDAP…), move them to their encrypted version (HTTPS, SFTP, SSH, LDAPS…) and change the exposed passwords.
Only accept HTTP Basic authentication over HTTPS: redirect HTTP to HTTPS and enable HSTS, or move to a stronger authentication method.

Disable automatic proxy detection (WPAD) by Group Policy if it is not used, or publish a controlled wpad record in internal DNS; prevent the wpad name from resolving externally so it cannot be hijacked.

Review the RADIUS server logs to tell a configuration error (shared secret, changed password) from a brute-force attack; fix the affected clients and, if needed, lock the targeted accounts and restrict the allowed sources.
Promptly analyse the reported processes (invalid or missing Authenticode signature) with the EDR or antivirus, check their origin and location, and isolate the machine if malware is confirmed.

Check that devices answering over Modbus/TCP or another unauthenticated industrial protocol sit in a dedicated network segment, allow access to them (TCP 502 for Modbus) only from supervision and engineering stations, and monitor these flows.

Apply the Secure Boot revocation list (DBX) update published by Microsoft and the manufacturer, then update the UEFI firmware and the boot loader. Test on a sample of machines first: an unsuitable DBX update can prevent booting.
